title: How to File Taxes with Unvested RSUs After Leaving US on H-1B: Complete Guide 2026
description: Navigate dual-country tax filing when you return to Canada with unvested RSUs. Learn Form 1040-NR requirements, treaty benefits, and avoid the $15K+ double taxation trap.
content:
## Key Takeaways

- You must file **both US and Canadian** tax returns for every year RSUs vest
- US Form 1040-NR required even if you're no longer a US resident
- Foreign Tax Credit prevents double taxation but **doesn't eliminate filing requirements**
- Average savings: **$12,000-$18,000/year** with proper treaty claims
- Failing to file US return = **30% withholding** on all RSU income (vs 0-22% with treaty)
- Use our [free calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator) for exact filing requirements

## The Post-Departure RSU Tax Situation

### What Happens When You Leave the US with Unvested RSUs

You worked 3 years at Amazon Seattle on H-1B. You received a standard 4-year RSU grant. Now you're returning to Toronto. Your 4th-year RSUs haven't vested yet.

**What most people think:**
> "I left the US, so no more US taxes."

**Reality:**
> You'll file **dual-country returns** for the next 1-4 years (depending on vesting schedule).

**Why:**
- US still claims tax on income you **earned** while working in the US
- Canada claims tax on income vesting while you're a **resident**
- Both countries have legitimate claims on the same income

### The Three Tax Years You Must Understand

**Year 1: Dual-Status Year (Year you leave)**
- Jan-Aug: US resident (H-1B status)
- Sep-Dec: Canadian resident
- File: US Form 1040 with dual-status statement + Canadian T1

**Years 2-4: Non-Resident Years**
- Full year: Canadian resident
- No US residency
- File: US Form 1040-NR (non-resident) + Canadian T1

**Year 5+: Canadian Only**
- All RSUs fully vested
- No US-source income
- File: Canadian T1 only

## Filing US Form 1040-NR: Complete Walkthrough

### Who Must File Form 1040-NR

**Required if:**
- You're a **non-resident alien** (no green card, not in US 183+ days)
- You have **US-source income** >$0 (including RSUs from US employer)
- You want to claim **tax treaty benefits** (Article XV)

**Deadline:**
- April 15 (if you had US withholding)
- June 15 (if no withholding, but interest accrues from April 15)

**Extension:** File Form 4868 by April 15 → extends to October 15

### Form 1040-NR Page 1: Income

**Line 1a: Wages, salaries, tips**

You must separate income into two categories:

**Column A: US-source income**
- RSU portion attributable to US work period
- Use work period attribution formula (see below)

**Column B: Non-US source income**
- RSU portion attributable to Canadian work period
- This portion is **exempt** from US tax (treaty benefit)

**Example:**
- Total RSU vested: $80,000
- Work period attribution:
  - US portion (75%): $60,000 → Report on Line 1a, Column A
  - Canada portion (25%): $20,000 → Exempt (don't report)

**Supporting docs:**
- W-2 from employer (shows full $80,000)
- Attach statement explaining $20,000 exclusion under Article XV

### Work Period Attribution Formula

The US-Canada tax treaty (Article XV) allocates RSU income based on where you **performed the work**.

**Formula:**
```
US portion = Total RSU × (Days worked in US / Total vesting period days)
```

**Example:**
- RSU grant date: Jan 1, 2023
- Vest date: Jan 1, 2027 (4 years)
- Total vesting period: 1,461 days
- Worked in US: Jan 2023 - Dec 2025 (1,095 days)
- Worked in Canada: Jan 2026 - Jan 2027 (366 days)

**Attribution:**
- US portion: $80,000 × (1,095 / 1,461) = **$60,000** (taxable in US)
- Canada portion: $80,000 × (366 / 1,461) = **$20,000** (exempt from US)

**Critical:** Keep a **daily work location tracker**. CRA and IRS **will** ask for proof during audits.

### Form 8833: Treaty-Based Return Position Disclosure

**When required:**
- You're claiming a treaty benefit that reduces US tax by **>$500**
- In our example: $20,000 exemption → $4,400 tax saved (>$500)

**How to fill out Form 8833:**

**Part I: General Information**
- Line 1: US taxpayer ID (SSN or ITIN)
- Line 2: Your name and address (Canadian address)
- Line 3: Check box (a) - claiming exemption from tax

**Part II: Treaty Article**
- Line 4: "Canada"
- Line 5: "Article XV(1) - Employment Income"

**Part III: Explanation**

Sample statement:

> "I am claiming an exemption from US taxation under Article XV(1) of the US-Canada Income Tax Treaty. The $20,000 of RSU income reported on my W-2 is attributable to services performed in Canada after I became a Canadian tax resident. This portion is exempt from US taxation per the treaty. The remaining $60,000 attributable to services performed in the US is reported as US-source income on Form 1040-NR, Line 1a."

**Attach:** Form 8833 to Form 1040-NR (Page 1)

**Penalty for not filing:** **$1,000** (if treaty benefit >$500)

### Schedule NEC (Tax on Income Not Effectively Connected)

Most H-1B workers' RSU income is **not** effectively connected with a US trade or business (you no longer work in US).

**Line 1: Income**
- Enter $60,000 (US-sourced RSU portion)

**Line 2: Tax rate**
- Treaty article rate: 0% (employment income exempt under Article XV if not performing services in US)
- But if still performing services in US remotely: 22-37% graduated rates

**In practice:**
- If you left US and work in Canada: **0% US tax** on vesting (already taxed via withholding at vest)
- Claim refund of **excess withholding**

### Claiming Refund of Overwithholding

**What happens at vesting:**
- Total RSU: $80,000
- Employer withholds: $17,600 (22% federal on full amount)
- But US can only tax $60,000 (treaty allocation)
- **You're owed refund:** $80,000 - $60,000 = $20,000 × 22% = **$4,400**

**How to claim:**

**Form 1040-NR, Line 25c: Federal income tax withheld**
- Enter: $17,600 (from W-2 Box 2)

**Form 1040-NR, Line 33: Tax**
- Calculate tax on $60,000 (US portion): ~$13,200

**Line 37: Refund**
- Withholding ($17,600) - Tax owed ($13,200) = **$4,400 refund**

**Processing time:** 6-12 weeks (IRS processes 1040-NR slower than regular 1040)

## Filing Canadian T1: Claiming Foreign Tax Credit

### Reporting RSU Income on T1

**Line 10400: Employment income**

Report **full** RSU amount (both US and Canada portions):

- Total RSU: $80,000 USD
- Exchange rate: 1.36 CAD/USD ([Bank of Canada annual average](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/exchange/))
- **CAD equivalent: $108,800 CAD**

**Why full amount?** Canada taxes worldwide income for residents. Even the US-sourced $60,000 is taxable in Canada.

### Form T2209: Federal Foreign Tax Credits

**Part A: Foreign non-business income tax**

**Line 40500: Net foreign non-business income**
- $108,800 CAD (full RSU in CAD)

**Line 40425: Foreign non-business income tax paid**
- US federal withholding: $17,600 USD
- Convert to CAD: $17,600 × 1.36 = **$23,936 CAD**

**Line 40600: Federal foreign tax credit**

Formula:
```
FTC = Lesser of:
  (a) Foreign tax paid ($23,936), or
  (b) Canadian tax × (Foreign income / Total income)
```

**Example:**
- Canadian tax on $108,800: $38,080 (35% marginal)
- Foreign income: $108,800
- Total income: $108,800 (RSU is only income)
- Calculation: $38,080 × ($108,800 / $108,800) = **$38,080**

**FTC allowed:** Lesser of $23,936 (a) or $38,080 (b) = **$23,936**

**Net Canadian tax owed:**
- Gross tax: $38,080
- Less FTC: $23,936
- **Payable: $14,144 CAD**

**Total tax (US + Canada):**
- US: $13,200 (on $60K portion)
- Canada: $14,144 (on $80K minus FTC)
- **Total: $27,344 USD** (34.2% effective rate on $80K)

**vs double taxation (if no FTC):**
- US: $13,200
- Canada: $28,160 (full tax, no credit)
- **Total: $41,360** (51.7% rate)
- **FTC savings: $14,016**

### Provincial Foreign Tax Credit

Most provinces (ON, BC, AB) allow provincial FTC for **both** US federal and state tax.

**Ontario Schedule 506: Ontario Foreign Tax Credit**

**Line 1: Foreign income**
- $108,800 (RSU in CAD)

**Line 2: Foreign tax paid**
- US federal: $23,936
- California state: $6,120 (if worked in CA)
- **Total: $30,056**

**Line 6: Provincial FTC**
```
FTC = Lesser of:
  (a) Foreign tax paid ($30,056), or
  (b) ON tax × (Foreign income / Total income)
```

**Calculation:**
- ON tax on $108,800: $12,142 (11.16%)
- Ratio: 100% (RSU is only income)
- **FTC limit: $12,142**

**FTC allowed:** Lesser of $30,056 or $12,142 = **$12,142**

**Net ON tax:** $12,142 - $12,142 = **$0** (full offset!)

## Multi-Year Filing Strategy

### Example: Google 4-Year RSU Grant Timeline

**Profile:**
- Hired: Jan 1, 2023 (H-1B in Mountain View, CA)
- RSU grant: $320,000 (4-year vest, $80K/year)
- Left US: Dec 31, 2025 (returned to Vancouver)
- Vesting dates: Jan 1 each year (2024, 2025, 2026, 2027)

**Filing requirements by year:**

**2024 Tax Year (Year 2 vesting: $80K)**
- Status: US resident (full year)
- File: US Form 1040 (resident) + CA Form 540
- No Canadian filing (not resident yet)

**2025 Tax Year (Year 3 vesting: $80K)**
- Status: **Dual-status** (resident Jan-Dec, left Dec 31)
- File: US Form 1040 with dual-status statement + CA Form 540
- File: Canada T1 (partial year resident, from Jan 1, 2026)

**2026 Tax Year (Year 4 vesting: $80K)**
- Status: Canadian resident (full year)
- File: **US Form 1040-NR** (non-resident) + **Form 8833** (treaty)
- File: **CA Form 540-NR** (non-resident, CA sourcing)
- File: **Canada T1** + **Form T2209** (FTC)

**2027 Tax Year**
- No RSU vesting
- File: Canada T1 only (if no US income)

### Tracking Matrix: What to File Each Year

| Year | RSU Vest | Status | US Federal | CA State | Canada | Forms Needed |
|------|----------|--------|-----------|----------|--------|-------------|
| 2024 | $80K | US resident | 1040 | 540 | None | 2 returns |
| 2025 | $80K | Dual-status | 1040 (dual) | 540 | T1 | 3 returns |
| 2026 | $80K | Canadian | 1040-NR + 8833 | 540-NR | T1 + T2209 | 4 returns |
| 2027 | $0 | Canadian | None | None | T1 | 1 return |

**Total filings over 4 years: 10 tax returns**

**CPA cost:** $1,500-$3,000/year for dual-country filing = **$4,500-$9,000 total**

**DIY with our calculator:** $0 (free) or $149/year (full filing suite) = **$447 total**

**Savings: $4,053-$8,553**

## Common Filing Mistakes That Cost Thousands

### Mistake 1: Not Filing US Return After Leaving

**What people think:**
> "I'm no longer a US resident, so I don't file."

**Reality:**
- You have **US-source income** (RSUs from US employer)
- US requires 1040-NR filing even if you owe $0
- Failing to file = **30% backup withholding** on all future US income

**Example:**
- 2026 RSU vests: $80,000
- You don't file 1040-NR
- 2027 RSU vests: $80,000
- Employer withholds **30%** = $24,000 (vs 22% = $17,600 normally)
- **Extra withholding: $6,400** (you might get it back... in 2028 when you file)

### Mistake 2: Not Filing Form 8833 (Treaty Disclosure)

**Penalty:** **$1,000** if treaty benefit reduces tax by >$500

**Example:**
- You claim $20,000 exemption under Article XV
- Tax saved: $4,400
- You don't file Form 8833
- IRS assesses **$1,000 penalty** + denies treaty benefit
- **Total cost: $5,400**

### Mistake 3: Using Wrong Exchange Rate for FTC

**IRS requires:**
- Use exchange rate **on date tax was paid** (not annual average)
- For withholding: use rate on vesting date

**CRA requires:**
- Use Bank of Canada **annual average rate** for income
- Use **date of payment** rate for FTC

**Example:**
- RSU vests Jan 1: USD/CAD = 1.40
- Bank of Canada annual average: 1.36

**Correct filing:**
- US Form 1040-NR: Report $80,000 USD (no conversion)
- Canada T1: Report $80,000 × 1.36 = $108,800 CAD
- Canada FTC: US tax paid $17,600 × 1.40 = $24,640 CAD

**If you use wrong rate:**
- US tax: $17,600 × 1.36 = $23,936 (understated FTC)
- Lost credit: $24,640 - $23,936 = **$704**

### Mistake 4: Not Claiming CA State Tax in FTC

Canada allows FTC for **both** US federal and state tax. US only allows FTC for foreign **national** tax (not provincial).

**Example:**
- US federal tax: $13,200
- CA state tax: $5,580 (CA Form 540-NR)
- Total US tax: $18,780

**If you only claim federal FTC:**
- Canada FTC: $13,200
- Lost credit: $5,580

**Correct:**
- Canada FTC: $18,780 (federal + state)
- **Savings: $5,580**

### Mistake 5: Missing Deadlines

**US deadlines:**
- Form 1040-NR: April 15 (or June 15 if no withholding)
- Extension: File Form 4868 by April 15 → extends to Oct 15

**Canada deadlines:**
- T1: April 30 (or June 15 if self-employed)
- Extension: Generally not available (only in special circumstances)

**Late filing penalties:**
- US: 5% per month (max 25%) + interest
- Canada: 5% of balance + 1% per month (max 12 months)

**Example:**
- You owe $10,000 Canada tax
- File 6 months late
- Penalty: 5% + (1% × 6) = **11%** = $1,100
- Interest: 5% annual = $250
- **Total: $1,350 penalty**

## When to Hire a Cross-Border CPA vs DIY

**DIY with our calculator if:**
- Single employer W-2 + RSU income only
- No AMT, no ISOs (RSUs only)
- Total income <$300K/year
- You're comfortable with tax forms

**Estimated time:** 4-6 hours/year for dual-country filing

**Hire a CPA if:**
- Total income >$500K/year
- You have ISOs + AMT issues
- You worked in CA/NY (complex state sourcing)
- You're applying for Canadian PR (immigration tax issues)
- You have self-employment income or rental properties

**Average CPA fees:**
- US Form 1040-NR: $800-$1,500
- CA Form 540-NR: $400-$800
- Canada T1 + FTC: $600-$1,200
- **Total: $1,800-$3,500/year**

**When to switch from DIY to CPA:**
- You get an audit notice
- Your situation becomes complex (new income sources)
- You make a mistake and need to amend (CPA can help negotiate penalties)

## Action Checklist

**Before leaving the US:**
- [ ] Download all RSU vesting schedules (E*TRADE, Fidelity, Schwab)
- [ ] Request work location tracker from HR (badge swipes, office assignments)
- [ ] Calculate future US vs Canada tax allocation (use our [calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator))
- [ ] Open Canadian bank account (for tax payments)
- [ ] Get Canadian SIN (Social Insurance Number) for T1 filing

**Each year RSUs vest (until fully vested):**
- [ ] File US Form 1040-NR by April 15 (or Oct 15 with extension)
- [ ] File Form 8833 if claiming treaty benefit >$500
- [ ] File CA Form 540-NR if worked in California
- [ ] File Canada T1 by April 30
- [ ] File Canada Form T2209 claiming Foreign Tax Credit
- [ ] Save all returns + supporting docs for 7 years

**To track:**
- [ ] Daily work location log (for audit defense)
- [ ] Exchange rates used (IRS yearly average, Bank of Canada)
- [ ] RSU vesting dates and stock prices
- [ ] US and CA tax payment receipts

**If you miss a filing:**
- [ ] File immediately (late is better than never)
- [ ] Request penalty waiver ("reasonable cause" - first-time filer)
- [ ] Pay tax owed with filing (reduces interest)
- [ ] Consider IRS Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedures (if multiple years missed)
